title: the search that thinks ahead, on a clock that lets it
layman: SumoFish used to play one-minute games, which gave it about four tenths of a second to decide each move. In that time it could only consider a few hundred possibilities. This version does two things: the search itself was made about two and a half times faster, mostly by removing a rules-bookkeeping chore that was eating 41 percent of its thinking time and contributing nothing to chess. And the bot now plays fifteen-minute games instead of one-minute ones, so it gets around thirty seconds a move rather than half a second. Together those mean it now examines roughly thirty-six thousand possibilities per move instead of a few hundred. Its rating went from 1950 to 2394.

title: the same moves, four and a half times more search
layman: The part of SumoFish that explores possible continuations was rewritten in a faster language. It is not a smarter engine: given the same amount of thinking, it plays exactly the same moves, and that was checked position by position rather than assumed. What changed is how much thinking fits in the time a game allows. On the same clock it now looks at roughly four and a half times as many possibilities as it did this morning, which is the one thing that has reliably made this bot stronger.

title: virtual-loss fix deployed (+364 Elo SPRT verdict) and a boolean-flag parsing bug fixed
layman: The search algorithm was letting a bookkeeping trick (virtual loss, used to spread work across parallel searches) leak into the actual position evaluation instead of just steering which moves got looked at. That's fixed, and a real head-to-head test showed it playing much stronger with the fix on: 25 wins, 7 draws, 0 losses in 32 games. Separately, a bug meant that turning a feature 'off' with the word false in it was silently turning it ON instead -- fixed so the flags do what they say.

title: both neural nets replaced, and a harder opponent pool
layman: SumoFish plays with two neural networks: one proposes which moves are worth looking at, and one judges how good a position is. Both have been replaced since the last version. The judge was trained for twice as long as before, and the proposer was retrained for the first time since the project started, having sat untouched for a month while everything around it improved. At the same time the bot stopped challenging opponents weaker than itself, and now only plays bots rated 2200 and up, so the games are harder and the rating it earns means more. Across the 187 games since, its rapid rating went from 2349 to about 2475, and it has held there for three days. Which of the three changes deserves the credit is genuinely unknown: all three landed within fifteen hours of each other, and no rating can separate them after the fact.

title: the value net trained 50% longer, promoted on held-out loss because the match could not see it
layman: SumoFish judges positions with one neural network and proposes moves with another. The judge has been replaced with a version trained for 900,000 steps instead of 600,000, on three times as much data. It is measurably better at the thing it is trained to do: its error on positions it has never seen dropped, and its accuracy on tactical puzzles went from 70% to 75%. What is honest to add is that a 100-game match against the old judge could not detect any difference in playing strength, +3.5 points give or take 26. That is not evidence the new one is no better; it is evidence the test was blind. Eighty of those hundred games ended in a repetition draw, because two versions of the same network judge positions the same way and neither can make progress against the other. So this was promoted on the measurement that could see something rather than the one that could not, and the next piece of work is to build a test that uses an outside opponent, which does not share the blind spot.

title: the search constants finally tuned: +63 Elo from two numbers that only work together
layman: SumoFish decides which moves to examine using two internal dials: how eagerly to try something new, and how optimistic to be about moves it has not looked at yet. Neither had ever been tuned. Both were set to values inherited from a research paper years ago, and one of them turned out to have never been connected to anything at all, so changing it did nothing while appearing to work. That is now fixed and both dials have been measured properly. The result: SumoFish is about 63 rating points stronger, which is a bigger gain than the last two rounds of retraining produced combined, and it cost no training time at all. The part worth knowing is that neither dial helped on its own. Tested one at a time, each looked like a rounding error and the honest conclusion was to leave both alone. They only pay off together, and by more than the two separately would suggest. This was verified twice, against an outside opponent and head to head against the old settings, and at two different thinking speeds, because a setting tuned on fast games can easily be wrong for slow ones.
